title: I am who am (Exodus 3:14)
hookLine: the name God gives Moses at the burning bush

lines: A BUSH THAT DOESN'T BURN UP.
WHO SHOULD I SAY SENT ME?
cards: A shepherd on a mountain in the desert. A bush is on fire and doesn't burn up. A voice from it tells him to go back to Egypt, face Pharaoh, and lead a nation of slaves to freedom.
And he asks the most reasonable question there is: who should I say sent me? What's your name? A name tells you who someone is, or at least how to call them.
The answer Moses gets is hardly a name at all. Today: Aquinas.

teach.b: First, the answer. In the Douay-Rheims, God says to Moses: "I AM WHO AM." And then: tell the people of Israel, "HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you."
In Hebrew it's three words, ehyeh asher ehyeh, built on the verb to be. Scholars still debate how to translate it: I am who I am, or I will be who I will be.
Jews read and treasure this passage too, and traditionally don't pronounce the holy four-letter name God gives in the next verse. Second, a name that won't be pinned down.

teach.h: A NAME THAT ISN'T A HANDLE.
teach.b: This is a name that refuses to be a handle. The Catechism says it's both revealed and mysterious: God tells Moses who he is, and at the same time stays beyond grasping.

teach.h: NOT A BEING, BUT BEING ITSELF.
teach.b: Third, being itself. Thomas Aquinas called HE WHO IS the most fitting name for God. For him, God doesn't just have existence, the way a tree or a star has it.
God is existence. Everything else has its being on loan; God simply is. Remember young Merton on the train, nearly throwing out a philosophy book?
This was the idea that stopped him. The Catechism calls God the fullness of being. Fourth, the Gospel echo.

teach.h: BEFORE ABRAHAM WAS MADE, I AM.
teach.b: In John's Gospel, Jesus says: "Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I AM."
Christians hear in those words a claim to the name from the bush. Catholics take that to mean the God who simply is came close enough to be spoken to by name.

how: Catholics hear the burning bush read at Mass, and out of reverence the Church asks that the Hebrew divine name not be spoken aloud in the liturgy, where it is rendered as the Lord.

o: the theologian who called God being itself
the prophet who heard God at the burning bush
the monk who taught Merton to pray in silence

games.q: the burning bush — tap the pairs.

s: the name at the burning bush is easy to translate
scholars debate it: I am who I am, or I will be who I will be.
Aquinas taught that God is being itself
not one being among others, but existence itself.
and traditionally do not pronounce the holy name God gives in the next verse.

games.q: you're Moses at the burning bush. you ask God's name, so you can tell the people who sent you. what answer do you get?
o: a name like the gods of Egypt
games.why: "I AM WHO AM ... HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." a name that reveals God and still refuses to be a handle.

practice: On each out-breath, say quietly, inside: I am. Not I am busy, or tired, or behind; just I am, and notice that you simply exist, right now, without doing anything to earn it.
Catholics believe every moment of that existence is borrowed from God, who simply is; if you pray, you can rest there, held in being.

wordCard.voice: Aquinas, the theologian who called God's name at the bush, HE WHO IS, the most fitting name, because God simply is existence. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am who am, or I will be who I will be, from the verb to be.

carryVoice: Your line: being itself. No achievement needed, just: I am. Day two hundred ninety-five.
